revise.summary: I revised content/lessons/15-wizard.md against the 1.3.1 wizard SKILL.md, template.sh and docs/engineering/wizard.md. Every high and medium finding is fixed, plus most lows. The Site story is rebuilt from repo facts only: the old journal at d21fc2c, issue 02, PR #1's body, commit c226730 and git log. Everything only a session log could back is cut. The terminal Scene used to replay this site's wizard from log details. It now shows the invented shop's Stripe wizard, built from the template's own example stage, so it matches the chat Scene and uses no terms before they are explained. Two Final test questions and one Checkpoint are new, so every goal (including re-running) has a Final test question, with no Checkpoint duplicating one and right answers spread a2/b3/c3/d2. The Try it now works from zero on Windows: it uses Git Bash for the run, `cd ~/wizard-practice`, the known false browser warning (issue #963), `cat .env.practice`, Esc, and a paste instead of a type. The checklist items now match what the template actually does.

quiz.where: Final test, spot-agent-ran-wizard, stem "The agent runs `bash scripts/setup-wizard.sh` itself." (line 390), right option "The agent ran it; Ana should, in a real terminal." (line 395)
quiz.problem: The stem gives the answer away. It says the agent ran the script "itself", and the right option just repeats that. It is also the only option that touches who ran it. Two distractors are weak: (a) says to edit the library, which the Lesson forbids in two places, and (d) is about `gh` sign-in, which has nothing to do with pauses. Nothing tests the real misconception, which is that `!` in the prompt box would have worked.
quiz.evidence: Lesson line 390: "The agent runs `bash scripts/setup-wizard.sh` itself." Line 395: "The agent ran it; Ana should, in a real terminal." Line 158 teaches that `!` fails the same way: "Don't run it from Claude Code's prompt box with `!` ... it can't get your keystrokes there". The stem's behaviour checks out: run from the agent's Bash tool, `bash -c 'read -r x; echo "read rc=$?"; [[ -t 0 ]] && echo tty || echo not-tty'` printed "read rc=1" and "not-tty". So `pause` (template.sh:81 `read -r _ || true`) falls through, and `ask` returns 1 under `set -e` (template.sh:9, 115-116).
quiz.fix: Stem: "Ana asks the agent to start the new setup wizard so she can watch it in the chat. The output races past every "Press Enter" and stops at the first prompt. Spot the mistake." Replace option a with "- [ ] She should have typed it after `!` in the prompt box instead." and feedback "  > `!` runs it from the chat too, so the pauses still get no keystrokes. That's how this site's author first ran his." Change the right option to "- [x] It ran from the chat; she needs a terminal window." and feedback "  > Right. A wizard waits for your Enter presses and typed values, and a script started from the chat can't get your keystrokes. The first real run is yours, in a window of its own." Keep b and d. Lengths: right 50, longest wrong 61.

quiz.where: Final test, spot-edited-library, stem "changing the hidden-typing helper in the library above the `STAGES` marker" (line 414), options b and c (lines 417, 419)
quiz.problem: The stem names the exact place ("above the `STAGES` marker"), and the right option is just its mirror ("below the marker"). Two distractors are weak. (b), the check going in `.env.example`, is refuted by a definition. (c), the agent running the wizard, is the same misconception refuted in five other questions. The stem also reuses the body's own Stripe example, so it tests recall, not transfer. The tempting wrong idea, that putting a check in the shared library is good reuse, is never offered.
quiz.evidence: Lesson line 414: "...in the library above the `STAGES` marker. Spot the mistake." Line 421: "The check belongs below the marker, in that stage." Stripe is the body's running example (lines 141-192, and template.sh:205-217). SKILL.md:10: "The library above the `STAGES` marker is identical in every wizard; that consistency is the point: never hand-edit it." The writing guide's pilot notes say: "Use a fresh situation ... not the body's own example sentence. Don't restate the defining phrase of the right answer in the prompt."
quiz.fix: Stem: "While writing a wizard for a maps service, the agent wants to reject any key shorter than 30 characters. It adds the check inside the hidden-typing helper in the template's library. Spot the mistake." Replace b with "- [ ] Nothing: in the library, every stage gets the check for free." and feedback "  > The library is identical in every wizard by design, so job-specific rules don't go there. Put the check in the stage that asks for the key." Replace c with "- [ ] Fine, if the agent makes the same edit in every other wizard." and feedback "  > Then every wizard needs hand edits to stay identical. Keep the library as shipped; a check for this one job goes in its stage." Keep a and d. Lengths: right 50, wrong options 49, 61, 61.

quiz.where: Final test, scenario-agent-can-do, stem "You're signed in to GitHub's `gh` tool on your laptop." (line 342), right option (line 343), options c and d (lines 347, 349)
quiz.problem: The right option is the only one that uses the stem's detail (`gh`), which is a wording tell. Distractors c (hidden typing for a step that captures nothing) and d (move the stage to the end) are irrelevant on their face, so only b competes. The stem also never says that your `gh` login is the agent's login. A cold reader has to infer it, though the Lesson's rule is about what "the agent is signed in to".
quiz.evidence: Lesson line 342: "You're signed in to GitHub's `gh` tool on your laptop." Line 343: "Create the repo yourself with `gh`; keep the wizard for the rest." Line 48: "If the agent is signed in to a command-line tool that can create the thing, it creates it." The feedback on c and d (lines 348, 350) admits neither option is about the real issue: "The problem is who should do the step" and "Order isn't the issue."
quiz.fix: Stem: "The agent works in your terminal, where you're signed in to GitHub's `gh` tool. Its setup plan includes a wizard stage: "Create a new GitHub repo in the browser." What do you say?" Right option: "- [x] "Do that one yourself; keep the wizard for the rest."" Replace c with "- [ ] "Keep it: steps that touch your GitHub account are yours to take."" and feedback "  > Your `gh` login already lets the agent do this, and it asks before it acts. Wizards are for steps it can't take." Replace d with "- [ ] "Keep it, but have the agent write the exact clicks for that stage."" and feedback "  > Precise clicks don't fix the real problem: the agent can create the repo itself, so it shouldn't be a stage." Lengths before quotes: right 51, wrong options 69, 64, 66.

quiz.where: Final test, scenario-rerun-after-fix, options b "Ask the agent to run the fixed wizard for you this time." (line 441) and d "Delete `.env` first so the fixed wizard starts clean." (line 445)
quiz.problem: Two of the three distractors repeat ones the cutover-stopped-halfway Checkpoint already refuted, in almost the same words. That leaves one live distractor (pasting values into the chat), which is weak too. The "agent runs the wizard" distractor also appears in five questions in all, so by the Final test it is a known-wrong pattern rather than a misconception. The real misconceptions about a re-run (that you must retype saved values, or that a changed script can't reuse them) go untested.
quiz.evidence: Checkpoint line 199: "Ask the agent to run the remaining stages itself." Line 201: "Delete `.env` so the re-run starts from a clean slate." Final test line 441: "Ask the agent to run the fixed wizard for you this time." Line 445: "Delete `.env` first so the fixed wizard starts clean." The "agent runs it" option also appears at line 92 (verify-before-handoff a), line 419 (spot-edited-library c) and line 433 (sequence-four-steps d), and spot-agent-ran-wizard is about it entirely. template.sh:94-104 and 111/124 show the defaults come from `$ENV_FILE`, not from the script, so any version of the script offers them back.
quiz.fix: Replace b with "- [ ] Re-run it and retype both saved values, so the fixed version has them." and feedback "  > No need: values already in `.env` come back as defaults, and Enter keeps them." Replace d with "- [ ] Start over in a new folder: a fixed script can't read the old one's values." and feedback "  > Saved values live in `.env`, not in the script, so any version of the wizard offers them back." Keep a (right, 57) and c. Wrong options: 70, 60, 75.

quiz.where: Final test, spot-pasted-in-chat, right option "The pasted copy is now in the model's context." (line 405), options c and d (lines 407, 409)
quiz.problem: The right option repeats the Lesson's highlighted defining phrase, so a reader can answer by recognition. Distractors c (use a visible prompt for a secret) and d (the key gets written to `.env` twice) are weak. Their own feedback concedes d "isn't the problem". Only a competes.
quiz.evidence: Lesson line 116 highlights the phrase: "==a key you paste into the chat is in the model's context==". Right option line 405: "The pasted copy is now in the model's context." Line 410 feedback on d: "And that isn't the problem." The writing guide's Questions rule: "no wording tells". Pilot notes: "Questions test transfer, not recognition."
quiz.fix: Right option: "- [x] That key is now exposed, whatever the wizard does with it." and feedback "  > Right. Anything pasted into the chat joins the model's context and goes to the provider's servers, and it can't be taken back, so make a new key and delete the old one. Describe values while scoping; type them only into the script." Replace d with "- [ ] The wizard should have asked for the key before scoping began." and feedback "  > Scoping comes before any script exists, and it never needs real values. Describe them instead." Lengths: right 58, wrong options 61, 57, 62.

quiz.where: Final test, scenario-credentials-wall, option b feedback "Code built on a fake key fails later, quietly." (line 334)
quiz.problem: No source backs the claim that a placeholder key fails "quietly", and it is arguably false: a fake API key usually fails loudly with an authentication error. The Lesson's own chat Scene also shows the agent carrying on building before it proposes the wizard. So a sharp reader can argue the placeholder route is not wrong in itself, and the feedback gives the wrong reason against it.
quiz.evidence: Lesson line 334: "Code built on a fake key fails later, quietly." Line 142, the agent in the shop Scene: "The checkout code and its tests are written, and I've added the two key names to `.env.example`." It keeps building, then proposes the wizard at line 144. Neither wizard/SKILL.md, docs/engineering/wizard.md nor the CHANGELOG says anything about placeholder keys.
quiz.fix: Feedback for b: "  > A placeholder only postpones the wall: the code can't really run until the real key exists, and only you can get it. Propose the wizard now."

quiz.where: Checkpoint which-belongs-in-wizard, options a "Installing the email library..." (line 52) and d "Writing the code that sends each alert email." (line 58)
quiz.problem: Three of the four options are plainly the agent's job (install a library, read public docs, write code). Only the right option mentions a "dashboard", a word the Lesson pairs with human-only steps throughout. That is a tell, and the Checkpoint never tests the boundary the section just taught: the agent does a job itself when it is signed in to a command-line tool, and key-related work is not automatically a wizard job.
quiz.evidence: Lesson line 48 (the section just read): "If the agent is signed in to a command-line tool that can create the thing, it creates it." Right option line 56: "Creating an API key in the email service's dashboard." "Dashboard" also appears at lines 22, 24, 27, 40 and 144. The writing guide says distractors must be "real misconceptions".
quiz.fix: Replace a with "- [ ] Creating the alerts database with a command-line tool the agent is signed in to." and feedback "  > If the agent is signed in to a tool that can create it, it creates it. No human needed." Replace d with "- [ ] Writing the code that reads the new key from `.env`." and feedback "  > Key-related doesn't mean human-only. Editing project files is the agent's job; only getting the key needs your login." Keep b and c. The right option (53) is still not the longest.

quiz.where: Final test, scenario-not-for-deciding, stem "Which Skill do you reach for first?" (line 354), option d (line 361)
quiz.problem: The word "first" invites a sharp reader to argue for `/setup-matt-pocock-skills`, which the course's own facts say runs once per repo before anything else. Its option text misdescribes the Skill and so stays wrong, but the stem shouldn't open that argument.
quiz.evidence: Writing guide, Facts: "`/setup-matt-pocock-skills` once per repo first." Lesson line 354: "Which Skill do you reach for first?"
quiz.fix: Stem ending: "Which Skill helps you make that decision?"

quiz.where: Checkpoint cutover-stopped-halfway, stem "Your wizard moves each customer's files to a new storage service, one batch per stage" (line 196)
quiz.problem: As written, the script moves the files by itself, with no human step. That is work the agent could do, so the example breaks the Lesson's own rule about what belongs in a wizard. A wizard cutover should put each irreversible step behind your yes.
quiz.evidence: Lesson line 48: "==If the agent can do it, the agent should do it==; a wizard is only for the logins, clicks and approvals that genuinely need you." SKILL.md:37: "`confirm` before any irreversible action". Pilot notes: "Worked examples must model the advice."
quiz.fix: Stem start: "Your wizard moves each customer's files to a new storage service, one batch per stage, each batch only after you type yes. Only the running script keeps track of which batches have moved."

quiz.where: Checkpoint verify-before-handoff, option c feedback "And a key should never pass through the agent." (line 97)
quiz.problem: The option is about a sample key, which is not a real secret, so the second reason doesn't apply and a reader can dismiss it. The first sentence alone is the real reason.
quiz.evidence: Lesson line 96: "Paste in a sample key to check that hidden entry works." Line 97: "That means running the wizard, which waits for a human. And a key should never pass through the agent."
quiz.fix: Feedback: "  > That means running the wizard, and it waits for a human at every prompt. The first real run, keys and all, is yours."

quiz.where: goals, fourth goal "re-run after a mistake and deleted when the job is done" (line 17); Final test scenario-keep-or-delete (line 377)
quiz.problem: The goal says "deleted when the job is done" with no exception, but the only Final test question on deleting asks about the exception and its right answer is "Commit it". As worded, the goal and the test key point opposite ways.
quiz.evidence: Line 17: "...re-run after a mistake and deleted when the job is done." Line 381: "- [x] Commit it and link it from the README." SKILL.md:12: "Commit it only when the user wants a repeatable setup path that should live in the repo."
quiz.fix: Goal: "- You'll be able to run a wizard safely: in a real terminal, with secrets typed into the script rather than the chat, re-run after a mistake, and deleted when the job is done unless the next person will need it."

reader.where: Try it yourself: "You need Claude Code installed and signed in (see [Start here](/learn/start-here))" (line 230) and step 6, "open Git Bash from the Start menu (it came with Git for Windows)" (line 258)
reader.problem: On Windows the exercise only works if Git for Windows is installed, but the Try it never lists it as a requirement. Step 6 just assumes Git Bash is there. A Visitor who has only Claude Code, the plugin and PowerShell finds no Git Bash in the Start menu, so they can't run the wizard (PowerShell can't run bash scripts, line 258). The agent may also have no bash, so the checklist item "The agent checked the script (`bash -n`...)" (line 277) can fail too.
reader.evidence: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup, 'Install on native Windows': "Installing Git for Windows is optional. It provides Git Bash, which the Bash tool and the Monitor tool need." and "Without Git for Windows, Claude Code runs shell commands via the PowerShell tool." The setup table lists Native Windows as "Requires: None; Git for Windows is optional". Start here does recommend it (content/lessons/00-start-here.md:35, "On Windows, install Git for Windows (git-scm.com)"), but this Try it doesn't say you need it.
reader.fix: Line 230: "You need Claude Code installed and signed in (see [Start here](/learn/start-here)). On Windows you also need Git for Windows (git-scm.com, also in Start here): it adds Git Bash, the bash terminal you'll run the wizard in, and lets the agent check the script. Use only made-up values: this is practice." Line 258: "On Windows, open Git Bash from the Start menu (Git for Windows installed it): PowerShell can't run bash scripts."

reader.where: Why it matters, big-idea callout: "Keys you type into the running script go straight into files on your machine and never pass through the model." (line 33)
reader.problem: This contradicts the rest of the Lesson. A secret typed into the wizard can also go to GitHub: the table's 'GitHub secret' and '`.env` and a GitHub secret' rows (lines 109, 111), line 116 ("goes from your keyboard into `.env` or GitHub"), and the terminal Scene's "✓ set GitHub secret STRIPE_SECRET_KEY" (line 185). A cold reader takes away from the headline callout that their keys never leave their machine, which is false whenever CI needs the key.
reader.evidence: template.sh:153-166, `set_secret` pipes the value to `gh secret set "$name"`, so it is sent to GitHub. SKILL.md:8 says it writes values "where they belong (`.env`, GitHub secrets)".
reader.fix: "The agent writes the wizard; you run it. Keys you type into the running script go straight to `.env` on your machine, or to GitHub, and never pass through the model."

reader.where: Try it yourself, the prompt: "Ask me for a made-up practice token with hidden input -> PRACTICE_TOKEN" (line 253); step 7, "type something fake like `test123` for the token" (line 265); checklist, "Your typing was invisible for the token" (line 280)
reader.problem: 'Token' appears here with no explanation. This course already teaches 'token' as the AI's unit of text, so a cold reader who has met that meaning won't see why a wizard asks for one. Here it means a secret access key, a meaning the Lesson never gives.
reader.evidence: content/lessons/02-context-window.md:30: "Models ... read tokens, not words: small chunks of text". The writing guide's pilot lessons (writing-guide.md:109) say token must be defined at first use. In 15-wizard.md the word appears only at lines 253, 265 and 280, never defined.
reader.fix: Use the Lesson's own word, key. Line 253: "3. Ask me for a made-up practice key with hidden input -> PRACTICE_KEY. Remind me to type a fake value." Line 265: "type something fake like `test123` for the key." Line 280: "Your typing was invisible for the key."

reader.where: Running it: "Open a new terminal window or tab (on Windows, Git Bash or WSL)" (line 158); also How Matt and others use it, "asked for PowerShell scripts instead of bash" (line 225)
reader.problem: Line 158 is the first use of Git Bash and WSL, and neither is explained. WSL is a bare acronym. Git Bash only gets a partial hint 100 lines later (line 258, "it came with Git for Windows"). A Windows Visitor doesn't know what to open. PowerShell is first named at line 225, also with no clause.
reader.evidence: grep of 15-wizard.md: first use of 'WSL' and 'Git Bash' is line 158 and of 'PowerShell' is line 225, none with a defining clause. Start here does define WSL (00-start-here.md:33, "WSL (Linux running inside Windows)"), but the guide requires each Lesson to stand alone (writing-guide.md:36, 109).
reader.fix: Line 158: "Open a new terminal window or tab (on Windows, use Git Bash, the bash terminal that comes with Git for Windows, or WSL, Linux running inside Windows), go to your project folder, and run the command the agent gave you." Line 225: "asked for PowerShell scripts (Windows' own terminal language) instead of bash".

reader.where: Try it yourself, prompt stage 2: "have me confirm I've read \"Ephemeral by default\"" (line 252), and step 8: "Run it again and press Enter at each prompt." (line 266)
reader.problem: The prompt says "confirm", which steers the agent towards the template's `confirm` helper. That helper is a [y/N] question, and pressing Enter counts as No. Step 8 tells the Visitor to press Enter at every prompt on the second run. If stage 2 is a `confirm`, the second run stops or loops at stage 2. Stage 3's prompt then never shows, so the checklist items "both value prompts offered [Enter keeps current]" (line 281) and "The last screen listed what it wrote" (line 283) fail.
reader.evidence: template.sh:84-90: `confirm` prints "[y/N]" and returns success only if the reply starts with y (`[[ "$reply" =~ ^[Yy] ]]`). template.sh:9: `set -euo pipefail`, so a bare `confirm` that gets No exits the script. SKILL.md:35 lists `pause`/`confirm` as the helpers the agent picks from. A plain Enter-to-continue gate is `pause` (template.sh:79-82).
reader.fix: Line 252: "2. Open https://www.aihero.dev/skills-wizard and wait for me to press Enter once I've read \"Ephemeral by default\" (a pure action, nothing saved)." Line 266: "Run it again and press Enter at each prompt (if it asks a [y/N] question, type y)."

reader.where: Why it matters: "can do a lot on its own, but it can't sign in to your accounts" (line 22), against The idea, What it's not for: "If the agent is signed in to a command-line tool that can create the thing, it creates it." (line 48)
reader.problem: The Lesson contradicts itself on its central distinction (goal 1). Line 22 says the agent can't sign in. Line 48 talks about the agent being signed in. The real rule, that the agent can use a login you already made in a command-line tool, is only implied later by the Site story (line 296) and the Final test (line 342, "You're signed in to GitHub's `gh` tool"). A cold reader can't tell whether *your* `gh` login counts as the agent's.
reader.evidence: 15-wizard.md:22, :48, :296 ("I was already signed in to GitHub and Vercel ... so it created the public GitHub repo"), :342-344 (the right answer has the agent use `gh` because *you* are signed in). SKILL.md:3: "Don't invoke this for steps the agent can perform itself."
reader.fix: Line 48: "If you're already signed in to a command-line tool that can create the thing (GitHub's `gh`, say), the agent runs it with your login and creates it itself."

reader.where: Common mistakes: "Check that `.env*` is listed in `.gitignore`" (line 290)
reader.problem: The pattern `.env*` also ignores `.env.example`, which the Lesson calls "a shared file" (line 66). In the chat Scene the agent adds key names to `.env.example` (line 142) so that later scoping can read them. A Visitor who follows line 290 would never commit that list.
reader.evidence: This repo's .gitignore:33-34 reads "# env files (can opt-in for committing if needed)" / ".env*", and `git ls-files | grep .env` lists no `.env.example`. Line 66 describes `.env.example` as the shared list of names.
reader.fix: "Check that `.gitignore`, the file of things Git ignores, lists `.env` (Next.js projects list `.env*`, which also hides `.env.example`; add a line `!.env.example` if you want to share that list)."

reader.where: Running it, terminal Scene: "Stripe setup" / "Ready to start?" (lines 172-173)
reader.problem: The Scene's banner leaves out the very promise that the prose (line 164, "The opening banner says you can stop and re-run any time") and the Checkpoint right after it (line 196, "The banner said you could stop and re-run any time") are about. The Visitor never sees that line in the Scene.
reader.evidence: template.sh:44-47: the banner prints "Stop any time with Ctrl-C and re-run later, since it remembers values already saved." before `pause "Ready to start?"`.
reader.fix: Insert a line between 172 and 173: "Stop any time with Ctrl-C and re-run later; saved values are remembered."

reader.where: Try it yourself, step 2: "type `/exit`, press Enter, install Matt's Skills, then run `claude` again:" (lines 240-244)
reader.problem: The colon after "run `claude` again" puts the install command right where a reader expects the `claude` command. The order of the two commands is also unclear, and the restart command is never shown on its own line.
reader.evidence: Lines 240-244: the sentence ends "then run `claude` again:" and the only code block after it is `claude plugin install mattpocock-skills@claude-plugins-official`.
reader.fix: "If not, delete it, type `/exit` and press Enter. Run this to install Matt's Skills, then type `claude` and press Enter to start again:" (keep the install block).

accuracy.where: ## A session, step by step, scene chat, line 151: "`bash -n` passes, shellcheck is clean, and the secret's name matches the one CI reads."
accuracy.problem: With the 1.3.1 template, a wizard can't come back clean from shellcheck. The template's own library has a line that shellcheck reports as an error, and the Skill forbids the agent to touch the library. So the Scene shows a check result that can't happen in 1.3.1. A Visitor who has shellcheck installed will see their agent report this error during the Try it and may think the wizard is broken, or watch the agent edit the library.
accuracy.evidence: template.sh:114 (library, above the STAGES marker): `[[ -n "$current" ]] && p+="$s$DIM$e[Enter keeps current]$s$RESET$e "`. Running `gh issue view 1295 --repo mattpocock/skills` shows the issue is OPEN, titled "wizard: template.sh prompt hits SC1087 — $e[...] parsed as an array subscript". Its body says "shellcheck 0.11.0 reports it as an error" and "Verified against HEAD `49dd158` (v1.3.1)". SKILL.md:10 says "never hand-edit it" and SKILL.md:37 says "Don't touch the library above the marker." The script still runs correctly: on bash 3.2.57 the string expands to `X\002[Enter keeps current]`, so only the shellcheck result is wrong.
accuracy.fix: Line 151: "Wrote `scripts/stripe-wizard.sh` from the template. `bash -n` passes, and the secret's name matches the one CI reads. I haven't run it: it opens your browser and waits for you." Optionally add to the Try it checklist item on line 277: "(if you have shellcheck, it may flag one line in the template's library: a known issue, which the agent should leave alone)".

accuracy.where: ## Try it yourself, step 4 prompt line 252 ("have me confirm I've read \"Ephemeral by default\"") with step 8, line 266: "Run it again and press Enter at each prompt."
accuracy.problem: The prompt asks the agent to make the Visitor "confirm" they've read the page. The template has a helper called `confirm`, a yes/no question that defaults to No. If the agent uses it, pressing Enter on the second run answers No. The script runs under `set -e`, so a bare `confirm` that gets No ends the run at stage 2 with no message. The run never reaches stage 3, so the checklist items "both value prompts offered [Enter keeps current]" and "The last screen listed what it wrote" fail. Whether this happens depends on which helper the agent picks.
accuracy.evidence: template.sh:84-90: `confirm "question" is a y/N gate; returns success on yes`, `read -r reply || true`, `[[ "$reply" =~ ^[Yy] ]]` (Enter gives an empty reply, which is a failure). template.sh:9: `set -euo pipefail`. template.sh:223: `run_wizard "$@"; exit` (a plain call, so `set -e` applies inside the stages). SKILL.md:35 lists `pause`/`confirm` among the helpers the agent uses. template.sh:78 says `pause` is the one that "waits for the human to confirm they've done the manual part".
accuracy.fix: Line 252: "2. Open https://www.aihero.dev/skills-wizard and have me press Enter once I've read \"Ephemeral by default\" (a pure action, nothing saved)." Line 266: "8. Run it again. Press Enter at each prompt to keep what's saved (if it asks a yes/no question, type y). Then run `cat .env.practice` ..."

accuracy.where: Common mistakes, line 290: "Check that `.env*` is listed in `.gitignore` ... (projects made with Next.js ... list it already)", against line 66: "`.env.example` (a shared file listing the names of the values `.env` needs...)"

Taken together, the advice makes `.env.example`, which the Lesson calls 'a shared file', invisible to Git. A new one won't be added by `git add`, so it isn't shared. The chat Scene (line 142) has the agent add key names to `.env.example`, which assumes the file gets shared.

Projects made with Next.js, a popular web framework, list `.env*` already, which also hides `.env.example`, so add a line `!.env.example` if you share one."
